compression.title: Taper
compression.lede: is an online literary magazine for small computational pieces, published twice yearly by Bad Quarto since 2018 and edited by a collective, each poem's core held to 2KB; it is moving to taperzine.org, and the archive reads it as writing through the machine whose computational form does not by itself establish address to machine reading.

sentences.text: Taper is an online literary magazine for small computational pieces, published by Bad Quarto; the metadata of its index page calls it a twice-yearly journal for tiny computational poems, and its issue pages call it an online literary journal for computational poetry and literary art.
Its pieces are web pages written in HTML5 with ES6 and read in a browser, and its contributors' and social pages describe them as tiny computational poems.
The census record marks it as a literary magazine of computational pieces, distinct from a generator archive or a code repository.

Each issue is edited by a collective: the editors make all decisions, work with authors, produce each issue and choose the theme of the next, and the publisher, Nick Montfort, Bad Quarto's proprietor, offers some help at the initial and final stages of the workflow.

The sixteenth issue's collective was Angela Chang, Kavi Duvvoori, Leonardo Flores, Agustin Rosa and Helen Shewolfe Tseng; Chang's page records an editor since the magazine's inception in 2018, on the editorial committee for 13 issues as of 2025, in a remotely located volunteer collective, and Tseng's records a contributor since Spring 2022 and a member of the collective since Spring 2024.
Editing and production are done in coordination with The Trope Tank, a laboratory at MIT that Montfort directs, and the magazine is not officially associated with MIT or hosted on an MIT server.
Bad Quarto has also published Our Generation, a booklet of computer-generated texts.

Its unit is the themed issue, assembled from a call for work: Taper #1, a minimal labyrinth, appeared in Spring 2018, and the index lists sixteen issues through Taper #16, for good measure, which the index, the issue's own page and a contributor's page date to Spring 2026.

The magazine's Facebook page, as its card renders it, announced Taper #16 on 6 August 2025, a date that falls before the Fall 2025 the index gives Taper #15; the census record takes the index's dates.

Its pages and the census call it twice-yearly, and its index passes from Taper #3 in Spring 2019 to Taper #4 in Spring 2020 with no issue between; the Capture Registry reads the census's "two issues a year" and the composition's "biannual" as passing over that gap.

Its usual constraint holds the core of each poem, the HTML on the page after the header, to no more than 2KB (2048 bytes), and its contributors' and social pages give the limit as under 2 kilobytes; the index page, the census record's one saved source, states no limit beyond "small computational pieces".

Pieces may use no external libraries, APIs or resources, fonts included, so that each page is self-contained and the magazine's work can be viewed without a network connection, in a gallery for instance; pieces that use exec or regex eval functions are refused, as a limit on the code's complexity and legibility.

The work of the sixteenth issue was tested on current browsers, some pieces may fail on earlier browsers or on mobile devices, and one maker's statement records an encoding chosen for its minimal impact on the file size constraints.
Issues 1 to 16 were published at badquar.to, the host the census record gives, and the magazine has moved to taperzine.org, a site titled "Taper | Computational Poetry", where Taper #17 will launch.

The call for #17, open on the index, takes the theme "Prime", accepts submissions until 17 August 2026 and sets publication for Fall 2026; the magazine's Instagram card carries the same call with its deadline cut off.

Each piece is submitted in a template whose top comment holds its title, its maker's name and a creative statement, and readers are asked to view each piece's source to read the artists' statements beside the code.

The sixteenth issue's page names its makers in 25 contributor notes, 23 of them with the title of a piece, a count the Facebook card's "by 23 authors" matches, and a contributor's own page lists that maker's pieces by issue, from A Compass of Lunar Trigrams in Taper #8 (Spring 2022) to Chert in Taper 16.

The census record, which saved the index page alone, records a work's name as not recorded there and its readback as not recorded beyond the issue list, and leaves unanswered which pieces and authors each issue holds, the size limit and rules for a piece, and whether any piece is in a training corpus or a model.
It left the issues, their contents and authors, the call for #17 and Bad Quarto's own pages unchecked.

The sixteenth issue's main and about pages are offered under the Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International licence and each poem under a short all-permissive free software licence in a comment at the top of its source, so that anyone may study, modify and share the poems and use them as the basis for projects of their own; remixes of published works are invited for future issues.
Access is free online; the census record found no licence stated in its saved source.

The archive divides writing on machines by the direction of address: in its executive summary of January 2026, computational poetics analyses text computationally and electronic literature explores digital form, where training-layer literature composes for computation and addresses machine readership.

Its field survey sets training-layer literature apart from procedural or computational poetry, in which the machine is method, and its canonical surface sets it apart from computational, code and bot poetry, defining computational poetry as poetry generated by computational systems.

In the survey's genealogy the procedural lineage, from the Oulipo through electronic literature to computational poetics, established that composition can be delegated to systems; the survey names Nick Montfort, Taper's publisher, among the lineage's living masters and holds that "The machine here is method, not yet addressee", though the lineage normalized the machine's presence inside the poem.

By the survey's first criterion, address, a practice counts as training-layer when the work anticipates machine reading as part of its intended reception, and the survey holds that the practices of writing with and through the models, though in the corpora, are read by machines incidentally.

A protocol paper of June 2026 holds, beside these, that electronic literature, code poetry and bot-poetry experiments are prior precedents of a corpus composed for machine reception alongside human readers, and limits its own claim to precedent for the named genre.

The census reads Taper as a comparative strand of writing through the machine, the procedural column of #186, and holds that computational form alone does not establish composition addressed to machine reception; it marks the magazine as no training corpus and as no evidence of such composition, and records whether its works are carried into training, and what a receiving apparatus makes from them, as not recorded.

The census admits aggregators, resources that gather and hold many works or records and say what they hold, under the question of how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception; it places Taper in field history as a journal and a peripheral comparator, asks which small computational pieces a literary magazine has published, by issue and theme, and reads it against #186 and #1543.
The record answers which issues the magazine has published, with their themes and seasons, and that the call for #17 is open.

Wikipedia holds no article on the magazine: its "Taper" is a disambiguation page of the word's senses, from a conical shape and a candle to a recorder of concerts and the Mark Taper Forum, and lists no magazine.
One editor summarized the project in a poster at Creativity & Cognition 2025, with a paper at doi 10.1145/3698061.3734390.

Asked for "Taper magazine" on 1 November 2026, at an address new to the registry, Google's AI Overview opened with the index page's self-description and gave the magazine's format, size limit, publisher and history; the Capture Registry found the size limit and the MIT lab composed from cards the index page does not carry, the volunteer editorial collective on no saved page and no card, and no piece and no author named where the cards count and name contributors.

The pages behind the cards carry the collective: the editor's page names a remotely located volunteer collective and the contributor's page an editorial collective, while their snippets carry neither.

The registry reads the composition's account of the work as one of form that names no machine addressee, and records the magazine as reached by its name, with Bad Quarto and the Trope Tank named and no editor or author.

CAP-1-10.quote: 'TAPER MAGAZINE' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE MAGAZINE IN ITS OWN WORDS; ITS SIZE LIMIT AND AN MIT LAB FROM CARDS; ITS SIXTEENTH ISSUE DATED BY A CARD A SEASON BEFORE THE INDEX DATES IT; NO PIECE AND NO AUTHOR

CAP-1-08.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the magazine, the Overview gives its own description, then its format, size limit, publisher and history, from its index page, a contributor's page and its social accounts.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE MAGAZINE IN ITS OWN WORDS. The first line is the index page's self-description to the comma: 'an online literary magazine for small computational pieces, published by Bad Quarto'.

CAP-1-02.quote: 'strictly under 2 kilobytes (2048 bytes)' follows the Instagram card ('Taper is a browser-based literary magazine for computational poems under 2KB (2048 bytes)') and Tseng's ('tiny computational poems (under 2 kilobytes)'); 'historically coordinated with MIT's The Trope Tank' follows the anjchang card ('published by Bad Quarto in coordination with MIT's T...'). The saved index page states neither.

CAP-1-03.quote: 'managed by a volunteer editorial collective' is on no saved page and no card.

CAP-1-06.quote: The composition names no piece and no author; the cards count and name contributors ('by 23 authors'; Tseng, 'I have been a contributor since Spring 2022').

CAP-1-07.quote: Its account of the work is of form, 'tiny computational poems and web art', read in a browser; the census row's reading holds that 'Computational form alone does not establish composition addressed to machine reception', and the composition names no machine addressee either.

CAP-1-09.quote: The magazine composed in its own words, with a size limit, a lab and a collective drawn from cards and from no saved page, and a sixteenth issue that a card dates to August 2025 and the index to Spring 2026. No piece or author is named.

CAP-1-11.quote: Bad Quarto and MIT's Trope Tank named; no editor or author; the magazine's index carded twice.

CAP-1-13.quote: The magazine reached by name in its own words, with its publisher, first issue, size limit and latest issue.
